prevalence: 1% of children have Tourette disorder. 3-8 per 1,000 children. Males 3-4x more likely than females. Onset always before age 18.
ageOfOnset: Typical onset between ages 5-7 years. Motor tics usually appear before vocal tics. Tics must start before age 18 for diagnosis. Peak severity usually in early teens (ages 10-12).

Unlike anorexia nervosa, ARFID does not involve disturbance in body image or fear of weight gain.

name: Pica
description: An eating disorder involving persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances for at least one month. The behavior is developmentally inappropriate (not part of normal infant/toddler exploration) and not culturally sanctioned. Common substances include ice, clay, dirt, sand, paper, soap, cloth, hair, string, paint chips, or chalk.

prevalence: Exact prevalence unknown due to underreporting. Estimates: 4-26% in institutionalized populations, 8-31% in pregnant women (often ice eating), 10-32% in children. More common with intellectual disabilities (up to 25%).

name: Hypersomnolence Disorder
description: A sleep disorder characterized by excessive sleepiness (hypersomnolence) despite a main sleep period lasting at least 7 hours. Individuals experience recurrent periods of sleep or lapses into sleep within the same day, difficulty being fully awake after abrupt awakening (sleep inertia), and/or prolonged main sleep episodes of more than 9 hours that are non-restorative. The excessive sleepiness causes significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

prevalence: Approximately 1% of the general population. Equally common in men and women. Primary form (idiopathic hypersomnia) is rarer, affecting about 0.005-0.3%.
ageOfOnset: Typically begins in late adolescence or early twenties (15-30 years old). Can also begin in childhood or later in life. Often gradual onset over months to years.
courseOfIllness: Usually chronic and persistent. Symptoms may fluctuate in severity but rarely remit completely without treatment. Can lead to significant functional impairment in work, relationships, and quality of life. May stabilize over time but typically requires ongoing management. Associated with increased risk of accidents (driving, work-related).

name: Narcolepsy
description: A chronic neurological disorder affecting the brain's ability to regulate sleep-wake cycles. The hallmark symptom is excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks. Narcolepsy Type 1 includes cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions), while Type 2 does not. Other symptoms may include sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, and disrupted nighttime sleep.
symptoms: ["Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) - primary symptom", "Sudden, irresistible sleep attacks (falling asleep without warning)", "Brief sleep episodes lasting seconds to minutes", "Cataplexy (Type 1 only): sudden bilateral muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions", "- Ranges from subtle (drooping eyelids, jaw drop) to complete collapse", "- Triggered by laughter, surprise, anger, or excitement", "- Consciousness remains intact during episodes", "- Episodes last seconds to minutes", "Sleep paralysis: temporary inability to move or speak when falling asleep or waking up", "Hypnagogic hallucinations: vivid, dream-like experiences when falling asleep", "Hypnopompic hallucinations: vivid experiences when waking up", "Disrupted nighttime sleep with frequent awakenings", "Automatic behaviors: performing routine tasks without awareness or memory", "Difficulty concentrating and memory problems", "Microsleeps: brief, involuntary sleep episodes lasting seconds", "Symptoms worsen with boring, passive activities", "Brief improvement after naps (but sleepiness returns)"]

prevalence: Approximately 0.025-0.05% (1 in 2,000-4,000 people). Affects approximately 200,000 Americans, 3 million worldwide. Equally common in men and women. Often underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed.
ageOfOnset: Two peak onset periods: around age 15 (most common) and age 35. Can occur from early childhood to late adulthood. Average delay from symptom onset to diagnosis is 8-15 years.
courseOfIllness: Chronic, lifelong condition. Symptoms typically worsen for first few years after onset, then stabilize. Does not shorten lifespan but significantly impacts quality of life. Cataplexy frequency often decreases with age. Treatment can greatly improve symptoms but rarely eliminates them completely. Increased risk of accidents, obesity, depression, and cardiovascular disease.

name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
description: A serious sleep disorder characterized by repeated episodes of complete or partial blockage of the upper airway during sleep. During these episodes, the diaphragm and chest muscles work harder as the pressure increases to open the airway. Breathing usually resumes with a loud gasp, snort, or body jerk. These episodes can interfere with sound sleep, reduce the flow of oxygen to vital organs, and cause heart rhythm irregularities.

prevalence: Estimated 2-9% of adults, though many cases remain undiagnosed. Prevalence rises significantly with age and obesity. Men are 2-3 times more likely to have it than women, though the gap narrows after menopause.
ageOfOnset: Can occur at any age, even in children (usually due to tonsils), but most commonly onset is between ages 40 and 60. Prevalence increases significantly after age 60.
courseOfIllness: Chronic and often progressive if untreated. Severity can fluctuate with weight changes. Without treatment, it increases risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, and accidents. With effective treatment (CPAP), prognosis is excellent and risks reduce significantly.

name: Restless Legs Syndrome (Willis-Ekbom Disease)
description: A sensorimotor neurological disorder characterized by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable or unpleasant sensations. These symptoms typically occur or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity, such as sitting or lying down, and are partially or totally relieved by movement. The symptoms follow a circadian pattern, worsening in the evening or at night.

prevalence: Affects approximately 5-10% of adults in North America and Europe. It is twice as common in women as in men. Can affect children (often misdiagnosed as growing pains or ADHD).

courseOfIllness: Generally a chronic, progressive condition. Symptoms may fluctuate, with periods of remission in early stages. Over time, symptoms tend to become more frequent, last longer, and extend to other body parts (arms). Secondary RLS (e.g., pregnancy-induced) often resolves when the cause is treated.

name: Erectile Disorder (ED)
description: A sexual dysfunction characterized by a persistent or recurrent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. This condition must persist for approximately 6 months and cause significant distress. It can be lifelong or acquired, and generalized or situational.

prevalence: Prevalence increases steeply with age. Approximately 2% of men under 40, increasing to 40-50% of men over 60. Transient episodes are very common in all men.
ageOfOnset: Can occur at any age after puberty, but incidence rises significantly after age 50 due to comorbidities. Sudden onset in young men is often psychogenic; gradual onset in older men is often organic.
courseOfIllness: Course depends on etiology. Psychogenic ED can be resolved quickly with therapy. Organic ED (e.g., due to diabetes) tends to be chronic and progressive but manageable with treatment. Situational ED may resolve when the stressor or relationship issue is addressed.

The diagnosis requires that the symptoms cause clinically significant distress and are not better explained by inadequate stimulation.

name: Premature (Early) Ejaculation
description: A sexual dysfunction characterized by a persistent or recurrent pattern of ejaculation occurring during partnered sexual activity within approximately 1 minute following vaginal penetration and before the individual wishes it. It is the most common male sexual dysfunction and can be lifelong (primary) or acquired (secondary).

ageOfOnset: Lifelong PE begins at first sexual encounter. Acquired PE develops after a period of normal sexual functioning.
courseOfIllness: Lifelong PE is chronic without treatment but responds well to therapy/medication. Acquired PE may resolve if the underlying cause (e.g., prostatitis, ED, relationship stress) is treated. Condition is highly manageable.
